independence: Fresh isolated reader. Read only the supplied BRIEF.md, tasks_reader418.json and claims_reader418.json for project context and the exact primary source_path PDFs named in those tasks. No cards, earlier outputs/calculations/ledgers/plans/history, other project sources, browsing or delegation were used. Own text extraction, 150 dpi context renders, 300 dpi numerical-table/figure renders and independent calculations were generated for this check. No claims, cards or ratings were changed.
source_access: All 15 frozen tasks assessed: 14 have supplied original PDFs across 7 unique files and were source-checked; task 9 (Launiainen 2014, PMC4237191) has no supplied primary full text and is not-found for access only. Review articles were read as original review sources, not as independent primary validation of the studies they cite. Ketola is the supplied accepted manuscript, so PDF pagination was used. No absent supplements or cited original studies were substituted.

results.note: The mechanism and the authors' uncertainty are supported. Tightened the last sentence: the paper reports one autopsy sampling occasion per person and no serial post-mortem data; it does not explicitly declare that no other sampling ever occurred. This is an inference from the reported protocol and cases, whose location must accompany the Discussion. Case 4 does have a hospital sample from life, so 'no repeated post-mortem samples' must not become 'no before/after comparison'.
results.corrected_extracted: The authors argue that incomplete distribution during life, including arterial–venous differences, and the variable make-up of blood after death cannot fully explain the large site differences, while allowing incomplete distribution during life as a contributory factor. They propose diffusion after death along concentration gradients from organs holding high drug concentrations, especially liver and lung, into nearby vessels; they state that the cause remains unresolved and is probably multifactorial, with diffusion from solid organs the major proposed factor. The report describes one post-mortem sampling occasion per person, at autopsy, and presents no repeated post-mortem sampling, so the timing and mechanism of the changes are inferred rather than followed directly after death. Case 4 also has a separate blood sample from life.
results.corrected_locator: Materials and Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 254); Results, four case descriptions (pp. 254–259); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 260, continuing as the 1st paragraph on p. 261), 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs on p. 261

results.note: Confirmed from the 300 dpi Table 3 image and fresh cell extraction. Across-drug medians recompute to 1.27, 0.45, 0.985 (printed 0.99), 5.06, 2.86, 1.84, 2.03, 3.685 (printed 3.69), 4.25 and 5.52. Column N sums are 576, 356, 385, 1697, 401, 565, 185, 187, 71 and 537: total 4960. Oxazepam brain prints N=1 with a blank ratio, making 4959 results attached to printed ratios. These are specimen results, not 4960 distinct deaths; the summary median is not a pooled individual-case median. Methods PDF p.4 supplies the within-case calculation explicitly.

All stated values, N values, extrema and maximum/minimum comparisons reproduce independently. Ephedrine and sertraline both have vitreous ratio 0.03. Fresh extrema and exact arithmetic are saved in calculations_reader418.json. The statements concern between-drug medians, with N=1 or 2 at several extremes; they do not estimate an individual person's post-mortem change or uncertainty.

Confirmed against the full Limitations paragraph spanning PDF pp.7–8. 'Usually higher' is the authors' description of femoral concentrations in Tables 2 and 5 relative to the all-cause reference medians; missing cause-of-death, time and co-factor data are not negative findings. The manuscript supplied is an accepted manuscript, so PDF page labels are appropriate.

Independent Table 2 transcription gives 99 entries, 98 distinct labels, 83 entries with numeric parentheses but 82 distinct labels with them, and 16 labels without numbers. Nicotine (Cotinine-3) remains an ambiguous target, not an unambiguous nicotine ratio. The fresh comparison reproduces 17 above 1.10, 3 below 1/1.10 and 4 between, including the named categories. Its denominator is specifically 24 labels with a single numeric Leikin value and a numeric Ketola other-blood median; do not interpret this as the total number of labels occurring in both papers. Morphine (heroin) was mapped to Morphine and printed Trazadone to Trazodone; D-methamphetamine was kept separate. Different matrices/source sets prevent paired replication or correction-factor interpretation.

The four intervals and hospital treatment are confirmed on printed pp.254,255,257,259 (PDF pp.2,3,5,7). 'All samples' must be understood as all post-mortem samples; case 4 also has the separate hospital sample. The reported intervals imply 9.25−7.25=2 h from hospital sampling to death, although the text says approximately 1 h before cardiac arrest; do not silently equate arrest and death. The surrounding claim's 3.5–6.6-fold range reproduces for the stated systemic blood ranges. It should be called systemic: case 2 separately reports portal venous concentrations of 40.9,42.8,48.3 mg/L, higher than those range maxima, and its Figure 2 displays 11 systemic vessel samples, not all collected blood sites.

Confirmed as Darke and Zador's secondary account, including the printed 0.16 mg/L and the three survivor-comparison citations. Monforte's cited 1977 is a publication year, not established study years. Neither this review nor its reference entry identifies the Monforte cause assigners or blinding. The cited original studies were not supplied/read; this cannot be promoted into independent primary case validation. Michigan is stated in the review's separate contaminants paragraph on the same page.

The cells and percentages are correct; the location needs expansion. Table 1 gives preliminary row totals 2719 and 237, and cells 2454/265/115/122. Independently, 265/2719=9.746230...% and 115/237=48.523207...%. The opening Results prose instead labels the final column totals 2569 and 387 as the preliminary groups, an internal inconsistency; use the table and component case descriptions. The assumption that the assigned pathologist's cause is correct and the rule that illicit-drug presence counts as contributing except with class I processes are in the limitations paragraph on p.192, outside the frozen locator. This confirms a presence/attribution comparison, not concentration discrimination or an independently validated cause standard. The 48.5% is an editorial proportion among initially unsuspected cases, whereas the paper's printed 4.48% uses 115/2569.
results.corrected_extracted: Of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related, 2,454 had a drug-related final cause after full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology and 265 did not; of 237 deaths not suspected, 115 had a drug-related final cause and 122 did not (2,956 deaths, 2016–2021, after excluding people under 18, obvious lethal injuries and suicidal drug overdoses). Editors' calculation: 265 of 2,719 is 9.75%; 115 of 237 is 48.5%. This is a study of drug presence and final cause attribution, not of drug concentrations. Cause assignment by the pathologist is treated as correct, not independently validated.
results.corrected_locator: Methods/Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 189); laboratory methods and case definitions, Table 1, and Results component-classification paragraph (p. 190); Discussion limitations paragraph beginning “This study has some limitations” (p. 192)

results.note: primary full text unavailable in supplied files. No source_path was supplied, and no card, note, prior extraction, browser, download or alternate source was used. The toxicology-access/certifier statement therefore remains unverified here; this is not a finding that it is false or absent from an available paper. The surrounding Finnish numeric claims and rounded THC percentage likewise cannot acquire fresh primary verification from this check.

Confirmed in both Methods paragraphs on printed p.299 (PDF p.2). Broad inclusion/exclusion rules are stated. No search dates, screening counts or study-level appraisal method appear in the supplied review. Stated exclusion of synthetic cannabinoids should not be read as proof every selected case is unconfounded; Table 1 row 29 itself mentions recent synthetic-cannabinoid use.

Independently counted Table 1: 31 numbered publications/rows, 35 individuals (three Mouzak cases plus two each in Lindsay and Dwivedi), five women, ages 15–53. Six stroke/TIA cases are explicitly tabulated: three in row 5 and one each in rows 14,15,19; the narrative says five. Three possible Brugada cases (rows 18,20,28) and one myocarditis (row 30) reproduce. The counts 24 without CAD and 18 with biomarker-confirmed AMI are confirmed as the review's narrative counts, but its table does not fully specify a per-person CAD/biomarker classification allowing unique reconstruction of those two totals. Original case reports are unread. No unique repair of the six-versus-five discrepancy or causal attribution is justified, and the three TIA cases explicitly lack detected heart disease.

Confirmed as review-reported numbers, including its printed Mittleman interval 2.9–9.5 and DeFilippis 90% CI. The second-hour timing is from prose; the 0.6–5.1 interval is in Table 3, which labels the window 'within 2 h'. No primary interval was checked or repaired. The separate Desai prose mortality null is present and must not be erased by its Table 3 AMI association. The rows do not establish independent samples: Mittleman and Frost share 64 centers and 1989–1996 enrollment, and Frost names the Determinants of MI Onset Study; Mukamal's 45-center 1989–1994 cohort could overlap, but its exact overlap cannot be resolved from this review. Keep acute events, selected notifications, mortality and null findings separate. The 35 French reports and 9 deaths are notifications without a population denominator. Table 3's Reis mortality null and Lee comparison also prevent a clean '11 of 12 increased risk' tally.

The attribution criteria, timing caveat and blood-test requirement are supported. Corrected the final attribution to Tormey's cited discussion: the supplied review says 'Tormey discusses' and reference 80 is a paper about possible cardiac deaths and coroners; it does not establish that the advice was written by a coroner. The separate Table 2 Tormey case reports a coroner's finding, which must not be conflated with reference 80. Original Tormey material was not read. The laboratory detection range and historical attribution proposal are not a validated causal threshold or medical advice.
results.corrected_extracted: The review proposes criteria for attributing a death to a drug: exclude other reasonable or competing explanations and establish an understood mechanism, a concentration capable of causing death and a fit with the circumstances. For THC the authors say it may not be possible to provide a minimum blood concentration that might be regarded as causal because of delays from death to sampling; many, if not most, laboratories can detect 1–2 ng/mL in post-mortem blood, and lower values could most likely reflect use days earlier. A blood THC test, rather than urine cannabinoids or history alone, is required to link a death to recent use. The review relays Tormey's discussion as advising that cannabis could be contributory only with use within 2 h of the cardiorespiratory arrest, ideally with blood THC confirmed. The supplied review does not identify Tormey as a coroner, and the cited discussion has not been independently read.
results.corrected_locator: Discussion, 8th–12th paragraphs (p. 304), especially the paragraph beginning “Tormey discusses”; reference 80 (p. 306)

results.note: The review reports significant post-mortem THC falls in repeated femoral samples (ref 30) and separately higher femoral THC than antemortem values in its AM/PM discussion (collective refs 30,42). The 17 h mean and 1–292 h range are printed with 12 cited references, none ref 30. Corrected 'pooled from' because the supplied review provides no underlying timing values, weights or aggregation method: the statistic can be transcribed but not independently recomputed. Neither direction identifies redistribution uniquely, and these remain secondary descriptions without effect sizes; absent underlying articles/supplemental data were not treated as verified.
results.corrected_extracted: In human bodies sampled more than once, significant falls in femoral-blood THC after death were reported in one study (ref 30), among falls for several other substances; the review gives no effect sizes. Separately, for repeated-sampling studies where the interval was available or estimated, the review reports a mean of 17 h from death to the first sample (range 1–292 h), citing 12 references that do not include the THC study. It supplies no underlying timing values, weights or aggregation method, so that summary cannot be independently recomputed here or assigned to the THC study. Separately, section 5.2 reports higher THC in femoral blood after death than in samples from life (collective refs 30,42), without effect sizes. Antemortem elimination, incomplete absorption/distribution at the earlier sample, possible later drug administration, hospital selection and plasma/serum versus whole-blood differences limit such comparisons; neither a rise nor a fall alone is uniquely attributable to redistribution. The underlying THC articles and any absent supplemental material were not read.
results.corrected_locator: §5.1, paragraph 3, including the timing-summary reference list; §5.2, paragraphs 1–2 (p. 6)

results.note: Confirmed on printed p.50 (PDF p.4). The review says whole blood is usual for autopsy and serum usual clinically, gives 12–18% for ethanol and a 1.6 factor to calculate cannabinoid plasma concentrations from whole blood, citing refs 34–35. Those cited originals were not supplied/read. The source supplies no individual post-mortem THC validation of that conversion, so the qualification must remain.
